fields.name: watts
fields.label: Load
fields.hint: Running watts from the appliance label or the appliance list. For an AC or motor use its running watts, not the starting surge.

fields.name: volts
fields.label: Supply voltage
fields.hint: Pakistan's mains is 230 V single-phase and 400 V three-phase. Older labels say 220 V; the result is almost the same.

fields.name: mode
fields.label: Supply type
fields.hint: Almost every home is single-phase. Choose three-phase only for a three-phase connection and enter the line-to-line volts.

fields.name: pf
fields.label: Power factor
fields.hint: Use 1 for heaters, irons, kettles and geysers. Use about 0.8 for ACs, fridges, water motors and mixed home loads.

answer: A {{in.watts|int}} W load on a {{in.volts|int}} V single-phase supply draws about {{out.amps|2}} A at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}. Amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor). A pure heating load has a power factor of one, so a {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W heater draws {{ex.1.out.amps|2}} A, while an AC or motor of the same watts draws more.
how: {{in.watts}} W ÷ ({{in.volts}} V × {{out.pf|2}} power factor) = {{out.amps|2}} A. For three-phase the voltage is also multiplied by the square root of three. The power factor turns the real watts into the apparent power the supply must carry; a heater has a power factor of one, motors and ACs less.
key_facts: On a {{in.volts|int}} V single-phase supply, amps = watts ÷ ({{in.volts|int}} × power factor); at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}, {{in.watts|int}} W draws {{out.amps|2}} A.

A {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W heater, iron or kettle (power factor one) draws {{ex.1.out.amps|2}} A at {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V; a {{ex.3.in.watts|int}} W 1.5 ton inverter AC at a power factor of {{ex.3.in.pf|2}} draws {{ex.3.out.amps|2}} A.

{{ex.0.in.watts|int}} W at {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V and a power factor of one is {{ex.0.out.amps|2}} A; at {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V the same load draws slightly less, so a 220V label and a 230V supply give almost the same answer.
Three-phase at {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V line to line spreads the load over three wires: {{ex.4.in.watts|int}} W at a power factor of {{ex.4.in.pf|2}} is {{ex.4.out.amps|2}} A per line.

formula.text: I = P ÷ (V × PF)  (single-phase);  I = P ÷ (√3 × V × PF)  (three-phase)
lines: V = supply voltage: 230 V single-phase, 400 V line-to-line for three-phase
PF = power factor, 1 for heating loads, about 0.8 for motors, ACs and mixed loads

sections.h2: {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V amps calculator: is {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V different from {{in.volts|int}} V?
p: Barely. Pakistan's standard supply is {{in.volts|int}} V, but many appliance labels and older guides say {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V. The same {{ex.0.in.watts|int}} W load draws {{ex.0.out.amps|2}} A at {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V and a little less at {{in.volts|int}} V, a difference smaller than the day-to-day swing of the mains itself. Pick whichever voltage your label shows; a 220V and a 230V calculation lead to the same wire and breaker choice.

The {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V option is for the US and Canada, where the same watts draw roughly twice the amps. That is why a {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V heater needs a much thicker cable than a {{in.volts|int}} V one.

sections.h2: How many amps is {{ex.2.in.watts|int}} watts at {{in.volts|int}} V?
p: It depends on the power factor. A {{ex.2.in.watts|int}} W heating load (power factor one) draws {{ex.2.out.amps|2}} A at {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V. A {{in.watts|int}} W load with a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}, typical of an AC, fridge or a mixed set of appliances, draws {{out.amps|2}} A. Same watts, about a quarter more current.

This is why an appliance's current is sometimes printed as a higher figure than watts ÷ volts. The label amps include the reactive part of the load, which the meter does not bill but the wire must carry.

sections.h2: AC amps at {{in.volts|int}} V: why the power factor changes the answer
p: A 1.5 ton inverter AC runs at about {{ex.3.in.watts|int}} W. With a power factor of {{ex.3.in.pf|2}} that is {{ex.3.out.amps|2}} A at {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V. A non-inverter AC of the same size runs at more watts and also starts with a surge of several times its running current for a second or two, which is what trips an undersized breaker. Use the running amps for the cable and the generator and breaker tools for the surge.

Resistive loads are simpler. An electric iron of about {{ex.0.in.watts|int}} W, a {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W kettle or a geyser all have a power factor of one, so their current is just watts ÷ volts. That is why the table below lists the power factor next to each row.

sections.h2: Three-phase and {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V: the same calculator for other supplies
p: Switch the supply type to three-phase and choose the {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V line-to-line option. The formula gains a factor of the square root of three because the load is spread over three wires: {{ex.4.in.watts|int}} W at a power factor of {{ex.4.in.pf|2}} draws {{ex.4.out.amps|2}} A per line. Enter the line-to-line voltage ({{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V in Pakistan), not the phase-to-neutral {{in.volts|int}} V.

Most homes in Pakistan are single-phase; a three-phase connection is normal for large houses, shops and motors. If you are checking whether a load fits a single-phase meter, the single phase load calculator does that job.

examples.text: {{in.watts|int}} W ÷ ({{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|int}}) = {{out.amps|2}} A. An iron is a pure heating load, so the power factor is one.

examples.text: {{in.watts|int}} W ÷ ({{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|int}}) = {{out.amps|2}} A. A room heater, kettle or hot plate of {{in.watts|int}} W draws {{out.amps|2}} A continuously while it runs.

examples.text: {{in.watts|int}} W ÷ ({{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|int}}) = {{out.amps|2}} A for a heating load. The same {{in.watts|int}} W with a power factor of {{d.pf_mixed|2}} draws more; try it in the calculator.

examples.text: A 1.5 ton inverter AC runs at about {{in.watts|int}} W. {{in.watts|int}} W ÷ ({{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|2}}) = {{out.amps|2}} A running current. Starting is gentle for an inverter AC; a non-inverter AC surges well above this.

examples.text: {{in.watts|int}} W ÷ (√3 × {{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|2}}) = {{out.amps|2}} A per line. The square root of three appears because three-phase power is shared across three wires.

mistakes: Using a power factor of one for an AC, fridge or water motor. Their current is about a quarter higher than watts ÷ volts; use about {{d.pf_mixed|2}} unless the label says otherwise.
Using the phase-to-neutral {{in.volts|int}} V with the three-phase formula. Three-phase needs the line-to-line voltage ({{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V in Pakistan) and the square root of three.

Taking the running amps of a non-inverter AC or motor as its only current. The compressor or pump surges to several times this for a moment at start-up, which is what trips breakers and stalls generators.
Buying a breaker or wire equal to the calculated amps. Cables and MCBs need a margin above the running current; use the wire size and breaker size calculators for the final choice.
safety: The amps from this page decide cable and breaker size, so never pick a wire or MCB from this result alone. Add the margins the wiring calculators use and have a licensed electrician check and connect any new circuit.

faq.q: How many amps is {{ex.0.in.watts|int}} watts at {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V?
faq.a: {{ex.0.in.watts|int}} W ÷ ({{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V × a power factor of one) = {{ex.0.out.amps|2}} A for a heating load such as an iron. For a motor or AC with a power factor of about {{d.pf_mixed|2}}, the current is about a quarter higher.

faq.q: How many amps does a {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W heater draw at {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V?
faq.a: {{ex.1.out.amps|2}} A. A heater is a pure resistive load with a power factor of one, so the current is simply {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W ÷ {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V, and it draws that for as long as the element is on.

faq.q: How many amps does an iron draw at {{in.volts|int}} V?
faq.a: A typical dry or steam iron is about {{ex.0.in.watts|int}} W, which is {{ex.0.out.amps|2}} A at {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V and a touch less at {{in.volts|int}} V. Bigger steam irons are rated higher, so check the label.

faq.q: What is the {{in.volts|int}} V current calculation formula?
faq.a: Amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor). For a {{in.watts|int}} W load at {{in.volts|int}} V and a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}, that is {{out.amps|2}} A. For three-phase, multiply the line-to-line voltage by the square root of three as well.

faq.q: How many amps does a 1.5 ton AC draw at {{in.volts|int}} V?
faq.a: A 1.5 ton inverter AC running at about {{ex.3.in.watts|int}} W with a power factor of {{ex.3.in.pf|2}} draws {{ex.3.out.amps|2}} A. A non-inverter unit runs at more watts and briefly surges to several times that when the compressor starts.

faq.q: Can I use this calculator for {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V?
faq.a: Yes. Choose the {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V option for US and Canadian supplies. The same watts draw roughly twice the amps of a {{in.volts|int}} V supply, which is why appliances there need thicker cable and higher-rated breakers.

faq.q: How many amps is {{ex.4.in.watts|int}} W on three-phase {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V?
faq.a: {{ex.4.out.amps|2}} A per line at a power factor of {{ex.4.in.pf|2}}. Three-phase divides the load across three wires, so each carries far less than the same load would on a single phase.

faq.q: Which wire and breaker do I need for these amps?
faq.a: Use the running amps with the wire size calculator, which adds the cable length and voltage drop, and the breaker size calculator for the MCB. Both keep a margin above the running current; a licensed electrician should confirm the final choice.
